For he who performs first has no assurance that the other will perform afterward, because the bonds of words are too weak to bridle men's ambition, avarice, anger, and other passions, without the fear of some coercive power; and in the condition of mere nature, where all men are equal and judges of the justness of their own fears, no such coercive power can possibly be supposed. And therefore he who performs first only betrays himself to his enemy, contrary to that right (which he can never abandon) of defending his life and his means of living.

But in a civil state, where there is a power set up to constrain those who would otherwise break faith, that fear is no longer reasonable; and for this reason, he who by the covenant is to perform first is obliged to do so.

The cause of fear that makes such a covenant invalid must always be something that arises after the covenant is made — some new fact or other sign of the will not to perform; otherwise it cannot make the covenant void. For what could not hinder a man from promising ought not to be admitted as a hindrance to performing.

He who transfers any right transfers the means of enjoying it, so far as lies in his power. So a man who sells land is understood to transfer the herbage and whatever grows upon it; nor can the seller of a mill turn away the stream that drives it. And those who give a man the right of government in sovereignty are understood to give him the right of levying money to maintain soldiers and of appointing magistrates for the administration of justice.

To make a covenant with brute beasts is impossible, because not understanding our speech they understand nothing of and accept no transfer of right, nor can they transfer any right to another; and without mutual acceptance there is no covenant.

To make a covenant with God is impossible except by the mediation of such people as God speaks to — either by supernatural revelation, or by his lieutenants who govern under him and in his name — for otherwise we do not know whether our covenants are accepted or not. And therefore those who vow anything contrary to any law of nature vow in vain, as being a thing unjust to pay such a vow. And if the thing is commanded by the law of nature, it is not the vow but the law that binds them.

The matter, or subject, of a covenant is always something that falls under deliberation (since to covenant is an act of the will — that is, an act, and the last act, of deliberation), and is therefore always understood to be something to come, and judged possible by the one who covenants to perform.

And therefore, to promise what is known to be impossible is no covenant. But if what was thought possible later proves impossible, the covenant is valid and binds — not to the thing itself, yet to its value; or, if that too is impossible, to the unfeigned endeavor of performing as much as is possible. For no man can be obliged to more.

Men are freed from their covenants in two ways: by performance, or by being forgiven. For performance is the natural end of obligation; and forgiveness is the restoration of liberty, being a retransferring of that right in which the obligation consisted.

Covenants entered into through fear, in the condition of mere nature, are binding. For example, if I covenant to pay a ransom or render service for my life to an enemy, I am bound by it. For it is a contract in which one receives the benefit of life, while the other is to receive money or service for it; and consequently, where no other law (as is the case in mere nature) forbids the performance, the covenant is valid. Therefore prisoners of war, if they are trusted with the payment of their ransom, are obliged to pay it; and if a weaker prince makes a disadvantageous peace with a stronger out of fear, he is bound to keep it — unless (as has been said before) some new and just cause of fear arises to renew the war. And even in commonwealths, if I am forced to redeem myself from a thief by promising him money, I am bound to pay it, until the civil law discharges me. For whatever I may lawfully do without obligation, I may lawfully covenant to do through fear; and what I lawfully covenant, I cannot lawfully break.

An earlier covenant voids a later one. For a man who has passed away his right to one person today does not have it to pass to another tomorrow; and therefore the later promise transfers no right, but is null.

A covenant not to defend myself from force by force is always void. For (as I have shown before) no man can transfer or lay down his right to save himself from death, wounds, and imprisonment — the avoidance of which is the only end of laying down any right. And therefore the promise of not resisting force, in any covenant, transfers no right, nor is binding. For although a man may covenant thus: “Unless I do so, or so, kill me,” he cannot covenant thus: “Unless I do so, or so, I will not resist you when you come to kill me.” For man by nature chooses the lesser evil, which is the danger of death in resisting, rather than the greater, which is certain and present death in not resisting. And this is granted to be true by all men, in that they lead criminals to execution and prison with armed men, even though such criminals have consented to the law by which they are condemned.

A covenant to accuse oneself, without assurance of pardon, is likewise invalid. For in the condition of nature, where every man is judge, there is no place for accusation; and in the civil state, accusation is followed by punishment, which being force, a man is not obliged not to resist. The same is also true of the accusation of those by whose condemnation a man falls into misery — such as a father, wife, or benefactor. For the testimony of such an accuser, if it is not willingly given, is presumed to be corrupted by nature, and therefore not to be received; and where a man's testimony is not to be credited, he is not bound to give it. Likewise, accusations under torture are not to be reckoned as testimony. For torture is to be used only as a means of guesswork and light in the further examination and search for truth; and what is confessed under it tends to the relief of the one being tortured, not to the informing of the torturers. It therefore ought not to have the credit of sufficient testimony — for whether he delivers himself by true accusation or false, he does so by the right of preserving his own life.

Since the force of words (as I have noted before) is too weak to hold men to the performance of their covenants, there are in man's nature only two imaginable helps to strengthen it. These are either a fear of the consequences of breaking one's word, or a glory or pride in appearing not to need to break it. The latter is a generosity too rarely found to be relied on, especially in the pursuers of wealth, command, or sensual pleasure, who make up the greatest part of mankind. The passion to be reckoned upon is fear; of which there are two very general objects: one, the power of spirits invisible; the other, the power of those men one will offend by breaking faith. Of these two, though the former is the greater power, the fear of the latter is commonly the greater fear. The fear of the former is in every man his own religion, which has its place in the nature of man before civil society. The latter does not — at least not enough place to keep men to their promises, because in the condition of mere nature the inequality of power is not perceived but by the outcome of battle. So before the time of civil society, or in its interruption by war, there is nothing that can strengthen a covenant of peace agreed upon against the temptations of avarice, ambition, lust, or other strong desire, but the fear of that invisible power which each one worships as God, and fears as an avenger of their treachery. All therefore that can be done between two men not subject to civil power is to put one another to swear by the God he fears. This swearing, or OATH, is a form of speech, added to a promise, by which the one who promises signifies that, unless he performs, he renounces the mercy of his God, or calls upon him for vengeance on himself. Such was the heathen form: “Let Jupiter kill me else, as I kill this Beast.” So is our form: “I shall do thus, and thus, so help me God.” And this, with the rites and ceremonies each one uses in his own religion, so that the fear of breaking faith might be the greater.

From this it appears that an oath taken according to any form or rite other than that of the one who swears is in vain, and no oath. And there is no swearing by anything that the swearer does not think is God. For although men have sometimes used to swear by their kings, out of fear or flattery, they would thereby have it understood that they attributed divine honor to them. And swearing unnecessarily by God is just profaning his name; and swearing by other things, as men do in common talk, is not swearing but an impious custom, picked up from too much vehemence in talking.

It also appears that the oath adds nothing to the obligation. For a covenant, if lawful, binds in the sight of God without the oath as much as with it; if unlawful, it does not bind at all, even though confirmed by an oath.

chapters.title: Chapter XV. Of Other Lawes of Nature
paragraphs: From that law of nature by which we are obliged to transfer to another such rights as, being retained, hinder the peace of mankind, there follows a third: That men perform their covenants made. Without this, covenants are in vain and empty words; and the right of all men to all things still remaining, we are still in the condition of war.

And in this law of nature consists the fountain and origin of JUSTICE. For where no covenant has preceded, no right has been transferred, and every man has a right to everything; consequently, no action can be unjust. But when a covenant is made, then to break it is unjust. And the definition of INJUSTICE is no other than the not-performance of covenant. Whatever is not unjust is just.

[Justice And Property Begin With The Constitution Of Commonwealth.] But because covenants of mutual trust, where there is a fear of non-performance on either side (as was said in the previous chapter), are invalid, then although the origin of justice is the making of covenants, yet there can actually be no injustice until the cause of such fear is taken away — which, while men are in the natural condition of war, cannot be done. Therefore, before the names of just and unjust can have a place, there must be some coercive power to compel men equally to the performance of their covenants, by the terror of some punishment greater than the benefit they expect from breaking the covenant; and to make good that property which by mutual contract men acquire in recompense of the universal right they abandon. And no such power exists before the establishment of a commonwealth. This may also be gathered from the ordinary definition of justice in the schools: for they say that “Justice is the constant Will of giving to every man his own.” And therefore, where there is no “own” — that is, no property — there is no injustice; and where no coercive power has been set up — that is, where there is no commonwealth — there is no property, all men having a right to all things. Therefore, where there is no commonwealth, nothing is unjust. So the nature of justice consists in keeping valid covenants; but the validity of covenants does not begin until the establishment of a civil power sufficient to compel men to keep them. It is then also that property begins.

The fool has said in his heart that there is no such thing as justice — and sometimes also out loud — seriously claiming that since every man's preservation and contentment is committed to his own care, there could be no reason why every man should not do whatever he thinks conduces to it, and therefore that to make or not make, keep or not keep covenants is not against reason when it conduces to one's own benefit. He does not in this deny that there are covenants, that they are sometimes broken and sometimes kept, and that such breach may be called injustice and the observance of them justice. But he asks whether injustice, taking away the fear of God (for the same fool has said in his heart there is no God), may not sometimes stand with that reason which dictates to every man his own good — particularly when it conduces to such a benefit as will put a man in a condition to disregard not only the disapproval and reviling of others but also their power. The kingdom of God is taken by violence — but what if it could be taken by unjust violence? Would it be against reason so to take it, when it is impossible to be hurt by doing so? And if it is not against reason, it is not against justice; otherwise justice is not to be approved as good. From reasoning of this sort, successful wickedness has gotten the name of virtue; and some who in all other things have disallowed the violation of faith have allowed it when it is for the gaining of a kingdom. And the heathen who believed that Saturn was deposed by his son Jupiter still believed the same Jupiter to be the avenger of injustice — somewhat like a piece of law in Coke's Commentaries on Littleton, where he says that if the rightful heir to the crown is attainted of treason, yet the crown shall descend to him, and Eo Instante (at that very instant) the attainder is void. From such examples a man would be very ready to infer that when the heir apparent of a kingdom kills the one in possession — even his own father — you may call it injustice, or by whatever name you like, but it can never be against reason, since all voluntary actions of men aim at their own benefit, and those actions are most reasonable which most conduce to their ends. This specious reasoning is nevertheless false.

For the question is not about mutual promises where there is no security of performance on either side (as when no civil power has been erected over the promising parties — for such promises are no covenants); but either where one of the parties has already performed, or where there is a power to make him perform. There the question is whether it is against reason — that is, against the benefit of the other party — to perform or not. And I say it is not against reason. To make this clear, we should consider: first, when a man does something that, despite anything that can be foreseen and reckoned upon, tends to his own destruction, yet some accident he could not have expected may turn it to his benefit, such events do not make the action reasonably or wisely done. Second, in a condition of war, in which every man, for lack of a common power to keep them all in awe, is an enemy to every other man, no one can hope by his own strength or wit to defend himself from destruction without the help of confederates. Each one in the confederation expects the same defense from it that any other does. Therefore, anyone who declares that he thinks it reasonable to deceive those who help him can reasonably expect no other means of safety than what can be had from his own single power. He, then, who breaks his covenant — and consequently declares that he thinks he may with reason do so — cannot be received into any society united for peace and defense, except by the mistake of those who receive him; nor, when he has been received, can he be kept in it without their seeing the danger of their mistake. And a man cannot reasonably reckon upon such mistakes by others as the means of his security. Therefore, if he is left out of or cast out of society, he perishes; and if he lives in society, it is by the errors of other men, which he could not foresee or reckon upon, and consequently against the reason of his preservation. So all men who do not contribute to his destruction forbear him only out of ignorance of what is good for themselves.

As for the example of gaining the secure and perpetual happiness of heaven by any means — that is frivolous, since there is only one way imaginable, and that is not breaking, but keeping, of covenant.

And as for the other example, of attaining sovereignty by rebellion — it is plain that even if the outcome follows, it cannot reasonably be expected, but rather the contrary; and because by gaining it this way, others are taught to gain the same in the like manner, the attempt is against reason. Justice therefore — that is, keeping of covenant — is a rule of reason by which we are forbidden to do anything destructive of our life; and consequently a law of nature.

Some go further and would have the law of nature be not those rules which conduce to the preservation of man's life on earth, but to the attaining of an eternal happiness after death — to which they think the breach of covenant may conduce, and consequently be just and reasonable. (Such are those who think it a work of merit to kill, depose, or rebel against the sovereign power constituted over them by their own consent.) But since there is no natural knowledge of man's condition after death, much less of the reward then to be given to breach of faith — only a belief grounded on what other men say, that they know it supernaturally, or that they know those who knew them, who knew others, who knew it supernaturally — breach of faith cannot be called a precept of reason or nature.

Others, who allow the keeping of faith to be a law of nature, nevertheless make exceptions of certain persons — such as heretics and those who do not perform their covenants to others. This too is against reason. For if any fault of a man is enough to discharge our covenant once made, the same ought in reason to have been enough to have prevented its being made in the first place.

The names just and unjust, when applied to men, mean one thing; when applied to actions, another. Applied to men, they signify the conformity or non-conformity of their manners to reason. Applied to actions, they signify the conformity or non-conformity to reason, not of manners or way of life, but of particular actions. A just man, therefore, is one who takes all the care he can that his actions may all be just; and an unjust man is one who neglects this. In our language such men are more often called righteous and unrighteous than just and unjust, though the meaning is the same. So a righteous man does not lose that title for one or a few unjust actions that come from sudden passion or mistake about things or persons; nor does an unrighteous man lose his character for the actions he does, or refrains from doing, out of fear — because his will is not formed by justice but by the apparent benefit of what he is to do. What gives human actions the relish of justice is a certain nobleness or gallantry of courage (rarely found) by which a man scorns to be indebted for the contentment of his life to fraud or breach of promise. This justice of the manners is what is meant when justice is called a virtue, and injustice a vice.
But the justice of actions denominates men not just but guiltless; and the injustice of the same (also called injury) gives them only the name of guilty.

Again, the injustice of manners is the disposition or aptitude to do injury; and is injustice before it proceeds to act, and without supposing any individual person injured. But the injustice of an action (that is to say, injury) supposes an individual person injured — namely, the one to whom the covenant was made. So many times the injury is received by one man while the damage falls upon another. As when the master commands his servant to give money to a stranger; if it is not done, the injury is done to the master, whom the servant had previously covenanted to obey; but the damage falls on the stranger, to whom the servant had no obligation, and therefore could not injure. And likewise in commonwealths, private men may forgive one another their debts, but not robberies or other violences by which they are damaged. For the withholding of a debt is an injury to themselves; but robbery and violence are injuries to the person of the commonwealth.

Whatever is done to a man in conformity with his own will signified to the doer is no injury to him. For if the one who does it has not by some prior covenant passed away his original right to do what he pleases, there is no breach of covenant, and therefore no injury done him. And if he has, then his will to have it done, being signified, is a release of that covenant — and so again there is no injury done him.

Justice of actions is divided by writers into Commutative and Distributive; the former, they say, consists in arithmetical proportion, the latter in geometrical proportion. Commutative justice, they place in the equality of value of the things contracted for; distributive, in the distribution of equal benefit to men of equal merit. As if it were injustice to sell dearer than we buy, or to give more to a man than he deserves. But the value of all things contracted for is measured by the appetite of the contractors, and therefore the just value is what they are content to give. And merit (besides the merit that is by covenant — where performance on one part merits performance of the other, and which falls under commutative, not distributive, justice) is not due as a matter of justice; it is rewarded only as a matter of grace. Therefore this distinction, in the sense in which it is usually expounded, is not right. To speak properly, commutative justice is the justice of a contractor — that is, performance of covenant in buying and selling, hiring and letting to hire, lending and borrowing, exchanging, bartering, and other acts of contract.

And distributive justice is the justice of an arbitrator — that is, the act of defining what is just. In doing this, being trusted by those who make him arbitrator, if he performs his trust he is said to distribute to every man his own. And this is indeed just distribution, and may be called (though improperly) distributive justice; but more properly it is equity, which is also a law of nature, as shall be shown in due place.

As justice depends on antecedent covenant, so gratitude depends on antecedent grace — that is, on antecedent free gift. And this is the fourth law of nature, which may be put in this form: “That a man which receiveth Benefit from another of meer Grace, Endeavour that he which giveth it, have no reasonable cause to repent him of his good will.” For no man gives except with intention of good to himself, because gift is voluntary, and of all voluntary acts the object is, to every man, his own good. If men see they will be frustrated of this, there will be no beginning of benevolence or trust, nor consequently of mutual help, nor of reconciliation of one man to another; and therefore they must remain in the condition of war, which is contrary to the first and fundamental law of nature, which commands men to seek peace. The breach of this law is called ingratitude; and it has the same relation to grace that injustice has to obligation by covenant.

A fifth law of nature is COMPLAISANCE — that is, “That every man strive to accommodate himselfe to the rest.” To understand this, we may consider that in men's aptness for society there is a diversity of nature, arising from their diversity of affections, not unlike what we see in stones brought together for the building of an edifice. As that stone which by the roughness and irregularity of its shape takes more room from others than it itself fills, and because of its hardness cannot easily be made flat — and so hinders the building — is by the builders cast away as unprofitable and troublesome, so a man who by roughness of nature will strive to retain those things which to himself are superfluous and to others necessary, and because of the stubbornness of his passions cannot be corrected, is to be left out or cast out of society as a burden to it. For seeing that every man, not only by right but also by necessity of nature, is presumed to endeavor all he can to obtain what is necessary for his preservation, anyone who opposes him in this for the sake of superfluous things is guilty of the war that follows from it, and therefore does what is contrary to the fundamental law of nature, which commands him to seek peace. The observers of this law may be called SOCIABLE (the Latins call them Commodi); the contrary, stubborn, unsociable, peevish, intractable.

A sixth law of nature is this: “That upon caution of the Future time, a man ought to pardon the offences past of them that repenting, desire it.” For pardon is nothing but the granting of peace; which, though granted to those who persist in their hostility is not peace but fear, yet not granted to those who give caution for future time is a sign of an aversion to peace, and therefore contrary to the law of nature.
[The Seventh: That In Revenges, Men Respect Only The Future Good.]

A seventh is: “That in Revenges, (that is, retribution of evil for evil,) Men look not at the greatnesse of the evill past, but the greatnesse of the good to follow.” By this we are forbidden to inflict punishment with any other design than for the correction of the offender or the direction of others. For this law follows from the previous one, which commands pardon upon security of the future time. Besides, revenge without regard to the example and the good to come is a triumph or glorying in another's hurt, tending to no end (for the end is always something to come); and glorying to no end is vainglory, and contrary to reason. To hurt without reason tends to the bringing-in of war, which is against the law of nature; and is commonly called by the name of cruelty.

And because all signs of hatred or contempt provoke fighting — to the point that most men would rather hazard their life than not be avenged — we may, in the eighth place, lay down this precept as a law of nature: “That no man by deed, word, countenance, or gesture, declare Hatred, or Contempt of another.” The breach of this law is commonly called contumely.

The question of who is the better man has no place in the condition of mere nature, where (as has been shown before) all men are equal. The inequality that now exists has been introduced by the civil laws. I know that Aristotle, in the first book of his Politics, as a foundation of his doctrine, makes men by nature — some more worthy to command, meaning the wiser sort (such as he thought himself to be on account of his philosophy), and others to serve (meaning those who had strong bodies but were not philosophers as he was) — as if master and servant were introduced not by the consent of men but by difference of wit. This is not only against reason but also against experience. For there are very few so foolish that they would not rather govern themselves than be governed by others; nor, when those who are wise in their own conceit contend by force with those who distrust their own wisdom, do they always — or often, or hardly ever — get the victory. If, then, nature has made men equal, that equality is to be acknowledged; or if nature has made men unequal, yet, because men who think themselves equal will not enter into conditions of peace except on equal terms, such equality must be admitted. And therefore, as the ninth law of nature, I lay down this: “That every man acknowledge other for his Equall by Nature.” The breach of this precept is pride.

On this law depends another: “That at the entrance into conditions of Peace, no man require to reserve to himselfe any Right, which he is not content should be reserved to every one of the rest.” As it is necessary for all who seek peace to lay down certain rights of nature — that is, not to have the liberty to do everything they please — so it is necessary for man's life to retain some, such as the right to govern their own bodies, to enjoy air, water, motion, and the means of going from place to place, and all other things without which a man cannot live, or cannot live well. If, in this case, at the making of peace, men require for themselves what they would not have granted to others, they act contrary to the previous law that commands the acknowledgment of natural equality, and therefore also against the law of nature. The observers of this law are those we call modest, and its breakers, arrogant men. The Greeks call the violation of this law pleonexia (πλεονεξία) — that is, a desire of more than one's share.

Also, “If a man be trusted to judge between man and man,” it is a precept of the law of nature, “that he deale Equally between them.” For without that, the controversies of men cannot be settled except by war. He who is partial in judgment does what lies in his power to deter men from the use of judges and arbitrators, and consequently (against the fundamental law of nature) is a cause of war.

The observance of this law — by the equal distribution to each man of what in reason belongs to him — is called EQUITY, and (as I have said before) distributive justice. Its violation is called acceptance of persons, Prosopolepsia (προσωποληψία).

And from this follows another law: “That such things as cannot be divided, be enjoyed in Common, if it can be; and if the quantity of the thing permit, without Stint; otherwise Proportionably to the number of them that have Right.” For otherwise the distribution is unequal, and contrary to equity.

But there are some things that can neither be divided nor enjoyed in common. Then the law of nature, which prescribes equity, requires: “That the Entire Right; or else, (making the use alternate,) the First Possession, be determined by Lot.” For equal distribution is of the law of nature, and no other means of equal distribution can be imagined.

Of lots there are two sorts: arbitrary and natural. Arbitrary, when agreed on by the competitors. Natural, either primogeniture (which the Greek calls Kleronomia (κληρονομία), meaning “given by lot”) or first seizure.
And therefore those things which cannot be enjoyed in common, nor divided, ought to be adjudged to the first possessor; and in some cases to the firstborn, as acquired by lot.

It is also a law of nature: “That all men that mediate Peace, be allowed safe Conduct.” For the law that commands peace as the end commands intercession as the means, and to intercession the means is safe conduct.

And because, however willing men may be to observe these laws, questions may nevertheless arise about a man's action: first, whether it was done or not; second (if done), whether against the law or not against it — the former being called a question of fact, the latter a question of right. Therefore, unless the parties to the question covenant mutually to stand by the verdict of another, they are as far from peace as ever. This other, to whose verdict they submit, is called an ARBITRATOR. And therefore it is of the law of nature: “That they that are at controversie, submit their Right to the judgement of an Arbitrator.”

And since every man is presumed to do all things with a view to his own benefit, no man is a fit arbitrator in his own cause. And if he were ever so fit, yet, equity allowing equal benefit to each party, if one is admitted to be judge, the other must be admitted also; and so the controversy — that is, the cause of war — remains, against the law of nature.
[The Eighteenth: No Man To Be Judge, That Has In Him Cause Of Partiality.]

For the same reason no man in any cause ought to be accepted as arbitrator to whom greater profit, or honor, or pleasure plainly arises from the victory of one party than from the other. For he has taken (though an unavoidable bribe, yet) a bribe; and no man can be obliged to trust him. And so the controversy and the condition of war remain, contrary to the law of nature.

And in a controversy of fact, the judge, having no more credit to give to one than to the other (if there are no other arguments), must give credit to a third, or to a third and a fourth, or to more. Otherwise the question is undecided, and left to force, contrary to the law of nature.

These are the laws of nature, dictating peace as a means of the preservation of men in multitudes, and which alone concern the doctrine of civil society. There are other things tending to the destruction of particular men, such as drunkenness and all other parts of intemperance, which may therefore also be reckoned among those things that the law of nature has forbidden; but they are not necessary to mention and not pertinent enough to this place.

And although this may seem too subtle a deduction of the laws of nature to be noticed by all men — most of whom are too busy getting food, and the rest too negligent to understand — yet, to leave all men without excuse, the laws of nature have been summed up into one easy formula, intelligible even to the meanest capacity: “Do not that to another, which thou wouldest not have done to thy selfe.” This shows him that he has no more to do, in learning the laws of nature, than, when weighing the actions of other men against his own, they seem too heavy, to put them into the other side of the balance and his own into their place, so that his own passions and self-love may add nothing to the weight; and then there is none of these laws of nature that will not seem to him very reasonable.

[But In Effect Then Only When There Is Security.] The laws of nature oblige In Foro Interno (in the inward forum, that is, in conscience) — that is, they bind to a desire that they should take place; but In Foro Externo (in the outward forum, that is, in public action) — that is, to putting them into practice — not always. For a man who should be modest and tractable and perform all he promises in such a time and place where no one else does the same would only make himself a prey to others, and procure his own certain ruin, contrary to the ground of all the laws of nature, which is the preservation of nature. And again, he who observes the same laws toward one who does not observe them himself does not seek peace but war, and consequently the destruction of his own nature by violence.

And whatever laws bind in foro interno may be broken not only by an act contrary to the law, but also by an act according to it, in case a man thinks it contrary. For although his action in this case is according to the law, yet his purpose, where the obligation is in foro interno, is a breach.

The laws of nature are immutable and eternal. For injustice, ingratitude, arrogance, pride, iniquity, acceptance of persons, and the rest can never be made lawful. For it can never be that war shall preserve life and peace destroy it.

The same laws, because they oblige only to a desire and endeavor — I mean an unfeigned and constant endeavor — are easy to observe. For in that they require nothing but endeavor, anyone who endeavors their performance fulfills them; and whoever fulfills the law is just.

And the science of them is the true and only moral philosophy. For moral philosophy is nothing else but the science of what is good and evil in the conversation and society of mankind. Good and evil are names that signify our appetites and aversions, which in different tempers, customs, and doctrines of men are different. Different men differ not only in their judgment of what is pleasant or unpleasant to the taste, smell, hearing, touch, and sight, but also of what is in conformity with, or contrary to, reason in the actions of common life. Indeed, the same man at different times differs from himself, and at one time praises — that is, calls good — what at another time he dispraises and calls evil. From this arise disputes, controversies, and at last war. And therefore, so long as a man is in the condition of mere nature (which is a condition of war), private appetite is the measure of good and evil. Consequently, all men agree on this: that peace is good, and therefore also the way or means of peace — which (as I have shown before) are justice, gratitude, modesty, equity, mercy, and the rest of the laws of nature — are good; that is to say, moral virtues. And their contrary, vices, are evil. Now the science of virtue and vice is moral philosophy, and therefore the true doctrine of the laws of nature is the true moral philosophy. But the writers of moral philosophy, though they acknowledge the same virtues and vices, yet not seeing wherein their goodness consisted, nor that they come to be praised as the means of peaceful, sociable, and comfortable living, place them in a mediocrity of passions — as if not the cause, but the degree of daring, made fortitude; or not the cause, but the quantity, of a gift made liberality.

These dictates of reason men usually call by the name of laws, but improperly. For they are only conclusions, or theorems, concerning what conduces to the preservation and defense of themselves; whereas a law, properly, is the word of him who by right has command over others. Yet if we consider the same theorems as delivered in the word of God, who by right commands all things, then they are properly called laws.

chapters.title: Chapter XVI. Of Persons, Authors, and Things Personated
paragraphs: A PERSON is one “whose words or actions are considered, either as his own, or as representing the words or actions of an other man, or of any other thing to whom they are attributed, whether Truly or by Fiction.”
When they are considered as his own, he is called a natural person. And when they are considered as representing the words and actions of another, he is a feigned or artificial person.

The word Person is Latin; instead of which the Greeks have Prosopon (πρόσωπον), meaning “the face,” just as Persona in Latin means the disguise or outward appearance of a man, counterfeited on the stage — and sometimes more particularly that part of it which disguises the face, like a mask or visor. From the stage it has been transferred to any representer of speech and action, in tribunals as well as in theaters. So a person is the same thing as an actor, both on the stage and in ordinary conversation; and to personate is to act, or represent, oneself or another. He who acts another is said to bear his person, or to act in his name (in which sense Cicero uses it when he says, “Unus Sustineo Tres Personas; Mei, Adversarii, & Judicis,” “I bear three persons: my own, my adversary's, and the judge's”). In various contexts he is called variously: a representer, or representative, a lieutenant, a vicar, an attorney, a deputy, a procurator, an actor, and the like.

Of artificial persons, some have their words and actions owned by those whom they represent. Then the person is the actor, and he who owns his words and actions is the AUTHOR; in which case the actor acts by authority. For what is called an owner in speaking of goods and possessions (in Latin Dominus, in Greek Kurios (κύριος)), in speaking of actions is called Author. And as the right of possession is called Dominion, so the right of doing any action is called AUTHORITY. So by authority is always understood a right of doing any act; and Done By Authority means done by commission, or license from him whose right it is.

From this it follows that when an actor makes a covenant by authority, he thereby binds the author no less than if he had made it himself; and no less subjects him to all the consequences of it. And therefore all that has been said before (in Chapter 14) of the nature of covenants between man and man in their natural capacity is also true when those covenants are made by their actors, representers, or procurators who have authority from them — so far as is within their commission, but no further.

And therefore he who makes a covenant with the actor or representer without knowing the authority he has does so at his own peril. For no man is bound by a covenant of which he is not the author; nor consequently by a covenant made against, or beyond, the authority he gave.

When the actor does anything against the law of nature by the command of the author, if he is bound by an earlier covenant to obey him, then it is not the actor but the author who breaks the law of nature. For though the action is against the law of nature, it is not his; on the contrary, to refuse to do it is against the law of nature, which forbids breach of covenant.

And he who makes a covenant with the author by the mediation of the actor, not knowing what authority he has but only taking his word, is no longer bound if such authority is not made evident to him upon demand. For the covenant made with the author is not valid without his counter-assurance. But if the one who so covenants knew beforehand that he was to expect no other assurance than the actor's word, then the covenant is valid, because the actor in this case makes himself the author. And therefore, just as when the authority is evident the covenant binds the author and not the actor, so when the authority is feigned it binds only the actor; there being no author but himself.

There are few things that are incapable of being represented by fiction. Inanimate things, such as a church, a hospital, a bridge, may be personated by a rector, master, or overseer. But inanimate things cannot be authors, and therefore cannot give authority to their actors. Yet the actors may have authority — given them by those who are owners or governors of those things — to procure their maintenance. And therefore such things cannot be personated before there is some state of civil government.

Likewise children, fools, and madmen who have no use of reason may be personated by guardians or curators; but they cannot be authors (during that time) of any action done by them, any longer than (when they recover the use of reason) they shall judge it reasonable. Yet during the folly, he who has the right of governing them may give authority to the guardian. But this again has no place except in a civil state, because before such a state there is no dominion of persons.

An idol, or mere figment of the brain, may be personated, as the gods of the heathen were — personated by such officers as the state appointed, and holding possessions and other goods and rights which men from time to time dedicated and consecrated to them. But idols cannot be authors, for an idol is nothing. The authority proceeded from the state, and therefore before the introduction of civil government the gods of the heathen could not be personated.

The true God may be personated. As he was, first, by Moses — who governed the Israelites (who were not his, but God's people) not in his own name, with Hoc Dicit Moses (“Moses says this”), but in God's name, with Hoc Dicit Dominus (“The Lord says this”). Second, by the Son of Man — his own Son, our Blessed Saviour Jesus Christ, who came to reduce the Jews and induct all nations into the kingdom of his Father, not from himself but as sent from his Father. And third, by the Holy Ghost, or Comforter, speaking and working in the apostles — which Holy Ghost was a Comforter that came not from himself but was sent, and proceeded from them both.

A multitude of men is made one person when they are represented by one man, or one person, provided this is done with the consent of every one of that multitude in particular. For it is the unity of the representer, not the unity of the represented, that makes the person one. And it is the representer who bears the person, and only one person; and unity cannot otherwise be understood in a multitude.

And because the multitude is naturally not one, but many, they cannot be understood as one but as many authors, of everything their representative says or does in their name. Every man gives the common representer authority from himself in particular, and owns all the actions the representer does, in case they give him authority without limit. Otherwise, when they limit him in what and how far he shall represent them, none of them owns more than they gave him commission to act.

And if the representative consists of many men, the voice of the greater number must be considered as the voice of them all. For if the smaller number pronounce, for example, in the affirmative, and the greater in the negative, there will be negatives more than enough to destroy the affirmatives; and so the excess of negatives, standing uncontradicted, are the only voice the representative has.

And a representative of even number — especially when the number is not great — by which the contradictory voices are often equal, is therefore often mute and incapable of action. Yet in some cases contradictory voices equal in number may determine a question; as in condemning or absolving, equality of votes — even by not condemning — absolves; but the reverse is not true, that not absolving condemns. For when a cause is heard, not to condemn is to absolve; but to say that not absolving is condemning is not true. The like holds in a deliberation about executing immediately or deferring to another time: when the voices are equal, not decreeing execution is a decree of delay.

Or if the number is odd — three or more (men, or assemblies) — of whom every one has by a negative voice the authority to take away the effect of all the affirmative voices of the rest, this number is no representative. For by the diversity of opinions and interests of men it often becomes, and in cases of the greatest consequence, a mute person — unfit, as for many other things, so for the government of a multitude, especially in time of war.

Of authors there are two sorts. The first, simply so called — whom I have before defined as one who simply owns the action of another. The second is one who owns an action, or covenant, of another conditionally — that is, who undertakes to do it if the other does not do it at, or before, a certain time. These conditional authors are generally called SURETIES, in Latin Fidejussores and Sponsores; and particularly, for debt, Praedes; and for appearance before a judge or magistrate, Vades.
